walkthrough:
**Check the molecular formula and skeleton**

Both geraniol and linalool contain 10 carbons, one alcohol group and two alkene groups. Count them and you get the same molecular formula, $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{18}\text{O}$.

$$\text{geraniol} = \text{linalool} = \text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{18}\text{O}$$

**Rule out chain isomerism**

Chain isomers have a different arrangement of the carbon skeleton. Here both have the same basic chain: a 8-carbon chain with two methyl branches at the same places. So the skeleton has not changed.

**Locate the functional group and double bonds**

In geraniol the $\text{-OH}$ is on a primary carbon as $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ at one end, with the $\text{C=C}$ next to it. In linalool the $\text{-OH}$ is on a tertiary carbon in the middle as $\text{-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-}$, and the terminal group is now $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH-}$.

$$\text{geraniol: 3,7-dimethylocta-2,6-dien-1-ol}$$
$$\text{linalool: 3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-dien-3-ol}$$

**Conclude the isomer type**

Same skeleton, same functional group type, but different positions of the $\text{-OH}$ group and of the $\text{C=C}$ double bond. That is the definition of positional isomerism.

options.A: Chain isomers need a different carbon skeleton or branching pattern. Both molecules have the same 3,7-dimethyloctadiene skeleton, only the substituents have moved, so this is incorrect.
options.B: Geometrical (cis-trans or E-Z) isomers need the same connectivity with different spatial arrangement around a $\text{C=C}$ bond. Here the connectivity itself is different because the $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{C=C}$ positions change, so this is incorrect.
options.C: Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images with the same structural formula and a chiral centre in both. Geraniol has no chiral centre and the two structures are not mirror images, so this is incorrect.
options.D: Both are $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{18}\text{O}$ alcohols with the same carbon skeleton. The $\text{-OH}$ group moves from C1 in geraniol to C3 in linalool, and the double bond moves from C2 to C1. A change in position of the same functional group is positional isomerism.
